Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-03-04 15:00 PT
Duration: 38m
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Asha Patel (Elmira CTO), Mark Reynolds (Elmira Lead ML Eng), Tina Gomez (Elmira PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated):
Redwood hosted API demo focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming responses, key generation parameters (max_tokens, temperature, top_p), and retry/idempotency patterns. Customer (Elmira) is evaluating hosted option for clinical triage assistant; main concerns are latency SLOs, cost per 1k tokens, and PHI handling (data residency). Action items: send pricing + SOC2/security docs, share benchmark scripts, schedule POC scoping.

Topics: Hosted API overview; streaming vs non-streaming; core params and tradeoffs; retry and idempotency; Redwood Console + Optimize suggestions; security/compliance notes; next steps/POC scope.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Sofia from Redwood, AE on the account. We've got Liam, our solutions engineer, who will run the demo. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Asha: Good, thanks. Excited to see how this could fit with our triage workflow.
[00:10] Liam: Great, quick agenda: we'll show the hosted API for chat and text gen, demo streaming in the SDK, walk through common params and tradeoffs, then cover retries / idempotency and wrap with next steps. Sound OK?
[00:20] Tina: Yep, perfect. We're especially curious about latency and predictable costs.
[00:25] Mark: And PHI — how data is handled; any residency or dedicated options.
[00:29] Liam: Yep we'll cover that. Quick qual: what's your typical traffic profile and latency needs?
[00:35] Mark: Right now our prototype is ~2k qps during peak for short prompts, avg convo length 300 tokens. Latency target is p95 under 500ms for initial response. Cost is, uh, important; we're looking to keep unit cost down.
[00:47] Sofia: Good color — that maps to a hosted deployment for eval, maybe Dedicated later. We'll show how batching/caching and Optimize recommendations can help.
[00:55] Liam: Jumping in — here's a quick curl/SDK example. (screenshare) This is the Node SDK call for chat: client.chat.create({ model: 'redwood-1-chat', messages: [..], max_tokens: 512, temperature: 0.2, stream: true });
[01:10] Liam: Two quick notes on streaming: 1) stream=true returns token deltas as they generate, so you can render partial responses; 2) for reliability we expose both SSE and websocket endpoints. If you see a hiccup you get partial output and then resume/retry logic on the client.
[01:30] Mark: How do you handle dedupe / double-charging on retries? If a request times out and client retries, do we risk duplicate tokens billing?
[01:38] Liam: Great question. We recommend idempotency keys for non-streaming calls. For streaming, the flow is slightly different — we support an idempotency token on the create call and server-side de-dup for replays within a short window. For long running streams you can checkpoint the last received token and resume, or just design the client to request a new call and use merge logic. Billing uses request-level semantics; partial stream fragments are accounted differently — we'll share exact ledger examples. (note: transcript may mis-hear ledger as "ledge-her")
[02:05] Asha: Is there an SDK snippet for resumable streams?
[02:08] Liam: Yeah, in the examples repo. I'll paste it after. It's SSE-based: you open the stream, listen for data events, and handle a reconnect with the idempotency-key header. We'll send the sample.
[02:20] Tina: Can you walk params quickly — like temp, top_p, stop sequences — what are your recommendations for clinical text?
[02:26] Liam: Sure — for clinical triage we usually suggest lower temperature (0.0-0.3) to reduce hallucinations, use explicit stop sequences for structured outputs, and keep max_tokens constrained. Also, set top_p conservatively if you care about determinism. Presence/ frequency penalties depend on prompt drift — we'll show examples.
[02:45] Mark: Any builtin safety/guardrails? We want to avoid hallucinations with PHI.
[02:50] Sofia: We have quality monitoring in Redwood Optimize — you can tie prompt sets to evals and get regression alerts. Plus you can pin model versions and have rollbacks. For PHI, hosted retains request logs for X days by default but you can request shorter retention or use Private/Dedicated with customer-managed KMS.
[03:08] Asha: What's the SOC / compliance story?
[03:10] Sofia: We're SOC 2 Type II certified; we also provide ISO docs on request and have audit logs, SSO/SAML, RBAC. For sensitive workloads many customers go Dedicated or Private. We'll share the security packet.
[03:22] Mark: Ok thanks. Can we talk about cost tradeoffs — quantization/latency?
[03:26] Liam: Yes. For hosted we surface model performance profiles — e.g., redwood-1-1B quantized runs cheaper but with slightly higher latency variability; larger models cost more but handle complex clinical reasoning. Our Optimize module recommends quantization level + batching settings per traffic pattern to hit a target cost/latency. Note: sometimes the transcript recognizes "quantizashun" spelled weird in auto text.
[03:50] Tina: For retries, what's your recommended backoff? We prefer idempotent safety — exponential backoff?
[03:55] Liam: Exponential backoff with jitter, yes. For production we also recommend circuit-breakers at the app layer and graceful degrade: e.g., fall back to cached or shorter answer when models are unavailable. Redwood's smart routing can automatically route to fallback model variants to keep service up.
[04:12] Asha: Any language on SLAs for hosted?
[04:15] Sofia: Hosted has best-effort uptime; SLA is included with Dedicated. For enterprise we can discuss an SLA if you commit to a reserved usage tier.
[04:24] Mark: Could you show Console briefly — where we tune batching / see token-level cost?
[04:28] Liam: Sure — (switch) here's Console: per-route dashboards, token cost breakdown, p95 latency, and Optimize suggestions. For your traffic pattern we might recommend continuous batching at 20-50ms windows to improve throughput without hurting tail latency. You can toggle batching rules per route.
[04:50] Tina: That sounds promising. Any gotchas moving from prototype to Dedicated?
[04:55] Sofia: Mostly around data residency and network setup. Dedicated provides reserved GPU pools, VPC peering, and customer-managed keys. It takes a bit more ops to set up but gives predictable throughput and SLAs.
[05:06] Mark: Ok. For the demo can you run a streaming example and show latency numbers?
[05:10] Liam: Yep running a simple prompt now (screen). I'm hitting create with stream=true, messages include patient symptom text, max_tokens 256, temperature 0.1.
[05:25] [05:25] Liam: (partial stream) "...suggested triage: urgent care, schedule follow-up within 24 hours, possible red-flag: shortness of breath..."
[05:34] Mark: That's pretty snappy. What's p50/p95?
[05:36] Liam: On this model our p50 is ~120ms, p95 usually under 420ms for these short prompts in the region I'm hitting; I'll attach benchmark numbers. For longer contexts p95 grows as expected.
[05:50] Asha: How do you do batching without increasing tail latency?
[05:54] Liam: It's a balance — we do micro-batching windows (20-50ms) and continuous batching for long-lived streams; plus prefix caching and KV cache reuse. If you need strict p95 targets we route by latency policy to lower-batch or single-request lanes.
[06:12] Tina: What's the retry behavior if streaming breaks mid-response?
[06:15] Liam: If the socket drops you'll get a disconnected event; we recommend the client try to reconnect with the same idempotency key and server will either resume or re-generate; that depends on the model and window. Sometimes it's easier to request a new generation and dedupe on your app side. We'll send a sample reconnect pattern in the examples repo.
[06:34] Mark: Billing — do partial failed streams bill full tokens or partial?
[06:38] Sofia: We bill for tokens generated; partial outputs are accounted for. We'll share ledger examples, but generally retries that cause re-generation will increase cost — hence idempotency and client logic matter for cost control.
[06:52] Asha: Any limits on streaming connections? We might have thousands of concurrent websocket sessions.
[06:57] Liam: Hosted supports scaled concurrency but sometimes supporting thousands of persistent websockets is easier on Dedicated or via a gateway pattern. We can architect a proxy layer. We'll share architecture notes.
[07:12] Tina: Can you show a snippet for server-side retries / idempotency header?
[07:16] Liam: Sure: curl -H 'Idempotency-Key: <uuid>' -d '{"messages":...}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat/create. For the SDK there is client.chat.create(..., { idempotencyKey: '...' }). Also for streaming the header is respected for a short dedupe window.
[07:40] Mark: Great. Anything about function calling or structured output?
[07:43] Liam: We support function/tool calling — you can have the model return a JSON-like structure and Redwood can validate/normalize. For clinical outputs we suggest strong schema and validators to avoid free-text hallucinations.
[07:58] Asha: What's your recommended rollout approach for a sensitive workflow?
[08:02] Sofia: Canary rollouts, start with low-traffic route, enable Optimize monitoring and quality evals tied to prompt sets, then gradual ramp. If any regressions are flagged you can auto-rollback to previous model version.
[08:15] Tina: Ok this is helpful. Can you also share a pricing calc example for our expected 2k qps, avg 300 tokens per convo?
[08:22] Sofia: We'll run a sample unit economics sheet and send it — rough calc in the follow-up.
[08:27] Asha: Last Q: data retention — can we purge logs on demand?
[08:31] Sofia: For hosted we have configurable retention windows; we can also sign BAA and/or move to Private/Dedicated for stricter controls. We'll include retention options in the security packet.
[08:45] Mark: Thanks.
[08:46] [08:46] Liam: Ok wrapping — I'll paste the example code and benchmark script after the call.
[08:50] Sofia: Recap quick: we'll send pricing + SOC2/security docs; Liam sends examples/benchmarks; Elmira provides prompt set and traffic profile. Schedule POC scoping next Wed.
[09:00] Tina: Sounds good. Thanks both.
[09:03] Asha: Appreciate it.
[09:05] Sofia: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up.
